prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Between the hands, between the brows, Between the lips of Love-Lily, A spirit is born whose birth endows My blood with fire to burn through me; Who breathes upon my gazing eyes, Who laughs and murmurs in mine ear, At whose least touch my colour flies, And whom my life grows faint to hear. Within the voice, within the heart, Within the mind of Love-Lily, A spirit is born who lifts apart His tremulous wings and looks at me; Who on my mouth his finger lays, And shows, while whispering lutes confer, That Eden of Love's watered ways Whose winds and spirits worship her. Brows, hands, and lips, heart, mind, and voice, Kisses and words of Love-Lily,— Oh! bid me with your joy rejoice Till riotous longing rest in me! Ah! let not hope be still distraught, But find in her its gracious goal, Whose speech Truth knows not from her thought Nor Love her body from her soul.

# Love-Lily
*(A Refined Rendering)*

Between the hands, between the brows,
Between the lips of Love-Lily,
A spirit stirs whose sacred birth endows
My blood with flame that courses ceaselessly;
Who breathes upon my rapt and gazing eyes,
Who laughs and murmurs soft within mine ear,
At whose faint touch my very color flies,
And whom my life grows faint, enraptured, but to hear.

Within the voice, within the heart,
Within the mind of Love-Lily,
A spirit wakes who lifts apart
His trembling wings and gazes tenderly;
Who lays his finger gently on my lips,
And shows, while whispering lutes their secrets share,
That Eden where Love's gentle current slips—
Whose winds and spirits kneel in worship there.

Brow, hand, and lip; heart, mind, and voice—
Kisses and words of Love-Lily—
Oh, bid me in your radiant joy rejoice
Till restless longing finds its harmony!
Ah, let not hope remain forever wrought
With doubt, but find in her its gracious goal,
Whose speech knows no distinction from her thought,
Nor Love division from her deathless soul.

---

*Note: I've preserved Rossetti's original structure, rhyme scheme, and central imagery while elevating certain phrases for enhanced musicality and precision. If you'd like, I can provide a version that stays even closer to the original wording, or explain specific changes made.*
outputs.L2:
Amid her palms, upon her forehead, Along the mouth of Love-Lily, A soul comes forth whose emergence sets My veins ablaze with living fire; It stirs the air before my staring eyes, It chuckles softly near my ear, At its faintest touch my face grows pale, And my very breath falters to catch its sound.

Deep in her tone, deep within her chest, Deep in the thoughts of Love-Lily, A soul comes forth who spreads wide His quivering wings and gazes back at me; He rests his finger against my lips, Revealing, as whispered melodies exchange, That garden of Love's flowing streams Where every breeze and being bow to her.

Forehead, palms, mouth, chest, thoughts, and tone, The kisses and utterances of Love-Lily— Oh, command me to share your delight Until my restless yearning finds its peace! Let hope no longer wander in doubt, But discover in her its worthy end, She whose words hold no distance from her thoughts, Nor Love any gap between her flesh and spirit.
outputs.L3:
From the very touch of Love-Lily—her hands, the arch of her brows, the curve of her lips—there rises a spirit so potent that it seems to kindle the speaker's very blood into flame. This presence is not gentle in its initial effect; rather, it storms through his senses, overwhelming reason and composure alike, until he is left breathless before the sheer physical reality of her.

The consequences of this encounter are profound and visible. The speaker finds himself drained of color, his body betraying the tumult within as faintness overtakes him. Even the smallest gesture—a fleeting touch of her hand, the softest murmur from her lips—is enough to entrance him completely, binding his attention so thoroughly that he becomes helpless before her, a man suspended between rapture and surrender.

Yet alongside this fevered, physical spirit, another emerges—one born not from her form but from her deeper essence: her voice, her heart, her mind. This second spirit works differently, not through fire but through stillness. It quiets the speaker, hushing the chaos that her physical presence first provoked, and in that silence it unveils something greater—a vision of paradise, a realm of love so complete that all things, seen and unseen, bow before it in reverence and worship.

Caught between these two spirits—one of flesh, one of soul—the speaker turns to Love-Lily with a plea that unites both realms. He begs that every part of her, her physical form as much as her spoken word, might converge to grant him joy. He longs for an end to his restless yearning, seeking in her the resolution of a hunger that neither beauty alone nor voice alone can satisfy.

The poem closes upon this note of longed-for unity, offering an ideal in which no division exists between truth and utterance, between body and spirit. In Love-Lily, these seeming opposites are dissolved into a single, seamless whole—flesh and word, form and essence, become indistinguishable expressions of one perfect love, each affirming and completing the other.
outputs.L4:
# Love-Lily: A Contemplation on Transcendent Love

The poem unfolds as an intimate meditation, a lover's rapt address to his beloved, whom he names Love-Lily—a figure who exists at the threshold between the physical and the spiritual, the earthly and the divine. From the opening lines, the speaker is consumed not by abstract philosophizing about love, but by the immediate, sensory reality of the woman before him. Her hands become for him a source of wonder; her brows, a landscape upon which he reads the story of his own devotion; her lips, a locus of unspoken promise; her voice, a music that seems to reorder the very air around him; and her heart, the hidden chamber from which all her grace seems to emanate.

What distinguishes this poem is the way the speaker insists that Love itself—capitalized, personified, almost divine—resides within these physical attributes, using them as vessels through which to reveal itself to him. This is not mere infatuation with surface beauty, but a conviction that the beloved's body has become inhabited by something larger than herself, a spirit that uses her flesh as its instrument. As he contemplates each feature in turn, the speaker describes a cascading effect: his senses become sharper, more alive, more attuned to subtleties he might otherwise have missed. The world takes on new textures and depths simply because he is looking at her, thinking of her, breathing the same air as her.

This heightened sensory awakening does not remain merely aesthetic or intellectual—it stirs something deeper and more urgent within him: a longing that borders on the metaphysical. He begins to yearn not just for her presence, but for a kind of fusion with her, a desire to close whatever distance remains between his soul and hers. The poem traces this movement from admiration to ache, from contemplation to craving, suggesting that true love inevitably transforms the lover into a supplicant, someone who recognizes in the beloved a completion he cannot achieve alone.

This longing reaches its culmination in the poem's final movement, where the speaker turns his contemplation into supplication. He calls upon Hope itself, personified as a companion or guide, asking that it find its rest, its fulfillment, its very reason for being in her. This is a striking rhetorical turn: rather than simply hoping for happiness in his own life, he suggests that Hope as an abstract force should locate its purpose specifically in Love-Lily, as though she represents the fullest possible answer to human longing and expectation.

In this final plea, the poem arrives at its central celebration: the seamless unity within her of truth and thought, of body and soul. She is not divided, as so many idealized figures in love poetry are, into a beautiful exterior masking an uncertain or inaccessible interior. Instead, her physical being and her inner essence are presented as perfectly aligned, mutually reinforcing, indistinguishable from one another. Her truth is not separate from her thought, nor is her body separate from her soul—she embodies a wholeness that becomes, for the speaker, the very definition of ideal love.

Thus the poem moves from sensory particulars—hands, brows, lips, voice, heart—toward a philosophical and almost spiritual conclusion, using the specific and tangible to arrive at the universal and eternal. It suggests that authentic love is transformative precisely because it does not ask the lover to choose between the physical and the spiritual, the body and the soul, but instead reveals their fundamental unity in the beloved. Love-Lily becomes, in this sense, more than a woman to be admired—she becomes a living demonstration of love's power to reconcile opposites, to awaken dormant senses, to give shape and purpose to hope itself, and to offer the promise of a completion that the speaker could not otherwise imagine.
outputs.L5:
# Between Love and Lily

There is a particular kind of tenderness that exists in the space *between* things—between a thought and its expression, between a question and its answer, between one heartbeat and the next. Love often lives in these in-between moments, in the pause before someone speaks the words that matter, in the quiet after they've been said.

Lily understood this instinctively, though she could never have explained it in so many words. She simply felt it—the way morning light filtered through curtains felt like love, the way a familiar voice on the phone felt like coming home, the way silence shared with someone comfortable felt fuller than any conversation.

She used to wonder why love resisted definition, why it slipped between the fingers of language like water. Perhaps love isn't meant to be captured but experienced—found in the between spaces of a life, in the gaps between obligation and desire, between who we are and who we're becoming.

Lily learned this slowly, the way all true things are learned. Not through grand declarations but through small repetitions: a hand reaching for hers in the dark, a name remembered, a promise kept without fanfare. Love, she came to believe, isn't a destination or even a feeling exactly—it's a practice of showing up in the space between two people, again and again, until that space becomes something sacred.

In the end, perhaps this is what Lily would say if asked to define love: it exists between two hearts willing to stay present with each other, in all the ordinary, unremarkable moments that quietly become everything.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Rossetti-style poem titled "Love-Lily" celebrating a beloved's physical and spiritual union, using repeated anaphora like "Between the hands, between the brows."
counterfactuals.output:
**Love-Lily**

Between the hands, between the brows,
Between the meeting of the mouths,
Sweet Love hath spread his golden vows
And drawn our two souls into one house.
Between the shadow and the shine
Her hair falls like a wheaten sign,
And in her eyes the still depths drowse
With light no mortal noon avows.

Between the hands, between the brows,
I feel the pulse of hidden spring,
As if the earth beneath her boughs
Had learned a holier blossoming.
Her breath is like the lily's breath
That does not fear the touch of death,
For love has made immortal vows
Between the hands, between the brows.

Between the throat and where the heart
Lies folded like a listening dove,
I find the place where flesh and art
Are made the sacrament of love.
Her body is a written word
Whose meaning only souls have heard—
Not lust, but light; not sense, but part
Of that great hymn no tongue can chart.

Between the hands, between the brows,
The world grows still as evening falls;
Time bends beneath the lily's boughs
And silence sings within these walls.
I do not ask if flesh shall fade,
For in her flesh a soul is made
Manifest, as branches house
The bird that sings among their boughs.

Between the hands, between the brows,
Between the pulse and the still breath,
Love binds what neither disallows—
Nor time, nor distance, nor swift death.
So let the lily stand for this:
That in one flower, root and bliss,
Body and spirit twine their vows
Between the hands, between the brows.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.output:
**I. Of the Hair and the Brow**

Thy hair falls like a river wrought of gold
Where sunlight drowns and lingers, loath to leave,
And in its amber depths my heart has told
A thousand vows no waking lips conceive.
Thy brow, a temple carved of ivory,
Bears thought too pure for mortal tongue to name—
I kneel before its calm divinity,
A pilgrim lost, yet burning still the same.

**II. Of the Hands and the Form**

Thy hands, twin lilies drawn from Eden's bed,
Do move as though they wove some silent prayer;
Each slender finger, pale and softly led,
Has touched my soul and left its blessing there.
Thy form, a sculpture breathing warmth to stone,
Sways like the willow o'er some sacred stream—
I would be dust beneath thy feet alone,
If dust might hold the shadow of this dream.

**III. Of the Soul**

But deeper still than flesh or golden hair,
Thy soul burns bright, a lamp within a shrine,
Where truth and tenderness together share
A light that makes the darkest hour shine.
Through all the veils that flesh and time unroll,
I seek that flame no shadow dares to hold—
Oh, let my restless hope, that seeks its soul,
At last find rest within thy gracious goal.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

**The Spirit Wrought of Beauty**

From out the marble of her brow,
Where thought like moonlight softly gleams,
There rose a Spirit—born, I vow,
Of beauty's own diviner dreams.

It took its breath from parted lips,
Where crimson whispers scarce began,
And drank the nectar honey sips
From roses blooming for no man.

Her eyes, twin wells of sacred night,
Gave birth to stars within its gaze—
A being woven half of light,
Half of the flesh's warmer blaze.

It walks not as the earthly walk,
Nor speaks in tongues of common speech,
But in the silence of her talk
Teaches what angels cannot teach.

For in her form, so richly wrought,
Both flesh and soul do intertwine—
The senses drowning in a thought
That beauty's truth is half divine.

I touched her hand, and felt the fire
That mortal love alone can start,
Yet found within that pure desire
A holiness that stilled my heart.

Oh, Spirit born of woman's grace,
Half breath of heaven, half of earth—
Thou art the truth in beauty's face,
The soul made flesh in mortal birth.

So let me worship at the shrine
Where flesh and spirit are made one,
Where every kiss becomes a sign
That love and God are never done.

For she who wears such beauty's crown
Doth wear as well truth's sacred robe—
And when her lashes flutter down,
I see eternity's own globe.

Thus spirit, sense, and soul entwine
In one bright flame that cannot part—
Her beauty is itself a shrine,
Her love, the scripture of my heart.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of Dante Gabriel Rossetti about a muse named "Love-Lily," using rich, archaic diction and structured stanzas with a repeating refrain about her name.
counterfactuals.output:
**Love-Lily: A Litany**

Within the garden of my soul's desire,
Where lilies pale do guard the sacred gate,
I found the flame that feeds my heart's own fire—
A face wherein all beauty lay in wait.
Her eyes were wells where ancient sorrows swim,
And in her voice the seraphs learned their hymn:
*Love-Lily, Love-Lily, my heart's own psalm.*

Her hair, unbound, a skein of ember-gold,
Doth fall as autumn falls upon the vine;
Her throat, a tower carved in ivory old,
Where doves have nested since the world's first sign.
I wist not if she be of earth or air,
But know her name doth bless my every prayer:
*Love-Lily, Love-Lily, my heart's own psalm.*

Betwixt the rose and thorn she chose to dwell,
A saint enshrined within a mortal frame;
Her smile, a chime from some forgotten bell,
Rings soft and low the music of her name.
Ere I had loved, I knew not love was this—
A wound made whole, a sorrow turned to bliss:
*Love-Lily, Love-Lily, my heart's own psalm.*

Yea, though the years should wither all I own,
And time's slow moth devour my golden days,
Her name shall stand, a pillar carved in stone,
Whereon the pilgrim heart forever prays.
For in that name all beauty is made whole,
And in its sound I find my scattered soul:
*Love-Lily, Love-Lily, my heart's own psalm.*

Lo, I have seen her walk the orchard's edge
At dusk, when swallows stitch the failing light,
Her shadow long upon the fading hedge,
Her face a moon new-risen into night.
And though she pass as all fair things must pass,
Her name endures, unbroken as a glass:
*Love-Lily, Love-Lily, my heart's own psalm.*

So let the years unwind their weary thread,
And let the world forget what once did bloom—
I shall not fear to join the silent dead,
If but her name may follow to the tomb.
For what is death to one who yet may hold
The single word wherein his heart is told:
*Love-Lily, Love-Lily, my soul's own psalm.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output:
# To Love-Lily

Breathe on me, Love-Lily, breathe the word
That first stirred waters into speaking light—
Let your voice find the hollow where I've heard
Silence pretending it could pass for night.

I was a garden once, before you came,
Untended, green with waiting, half-asleep.
Now every leaf remembers your name
And roots grow bold in soil they used to keep

Hidden from touch, from sun, from anything
That asked the flesh to answer for the soul.
But you have taught my body how to sing
The song my spirit always meant as whole—

Not two things joined, but one thing come undone
Of its own hiding, one flame lit from one.

Your breath is Eden entering my breath,
The old walls falling where the angel stood
With flaming sword against the way of death—
Now every gate stands open, understood

As threshold, not as ending. In your voice
I hear the first light asking to be named,
And in your hands I find I have no choice
But to be human, wholly, unashamed.

Love-Lily, when you speak my name aloud
It is as if the world remembers why
It bothered blooming—why the humble cloud
Consents to break and water earth and sky.

Soul is not prisoner here, nor flesh its guard:
We are the garden and the gardener's word.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
